I have been farming here in Quzhou for nearly thirty years, ever since I left school after primary. My family has about 10 mu of good flat land, and I know every corner of it. Last year I grew winter wheat followed by summer maize on all of it, and that is what I will do again this year. My neighbors mostly do the same — it is the safest way here. I thought about cotton once, but the labor is too much and the price bounces around too much for my liking. 

For the wheat, I will plough the soil first and then do rotary tillage to make it fine for sowing in mid-October. I will buy improved seed — maybe the kind the government station recommends, like the ones Wang down the road used last year. I will put down compound fertilizer as base, about 18 kg of nitrogen per mu, 11 kg of phosphorus, and 4 kg of potassium. I know some young farmers say they use less nitrogen now, but I remember two years ago when my cousin cut back and his wheat turned yellow at jointing. I would rather not take that risk. I will irrigate four times: once before winter freeze, and three more times in spring when the wheat starts growing fast and the weather gets dry. I will spray pesticide four times — herbicide once, and insecticide two or three times as needed.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, there is barely a week before I must plant the maize. Everyone here does no-tillage for maize — there is simply no time to plough again. I will plant hybrid maize seed right into the stubble. For fertilizer, I will put about 12 kg nitrogen per mu, 3 kg phosphorus, and 3 kg potassium. Maize does not need as much as wheat, and the leftover wheat roots help the soil. I will irrigate twice for the maize, once at the big trumpet stage and once when the tassels come out, if the rain does not come. Pesticide three times should be enough — the main worry is the corn borer. If the weather is normal, I expect about 450 kg per mu of wheat and 500 kg per mu of maize. That is roughly what my good fields gave me two years ago.
